doc.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995

title: Early jazz in the 1920s and the Holy Rollers
summary: Asked whether jazz felt new, he describes the 1924 Nashville Holy Rollers as the start of rock and roll-like music.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Can I take you back to your early days in Chicago, and it seems that in music every once in a while there seems to be a time when something new happens fairly quickly, like with rock & roll in the late 50s, or some classical composer writing something brand new. When you were young, was jazz first called “jazz?” Do you remember what the music was, like you felt like you were into something really new here? Is that a fair statement?

Well, that is a fair statement. Because as I said before, back then in the 20s, my goodness, rock & roll was never heard of. But there were people that sound like rock & roll back in the 20s, as far as 1924 in Nashville. We had people called “Holy Rollers.” They had tents. And every night that’s all you could hear, was people rolling on the ground and singing and, that’s all there was. Singing old blues and groaning, and they called them “Holy Rollers.” That’s the beginning of all this stuff. That’s the beginning.
